pillar: Liver RFA in China: Zhongshan Hospital, EHBH, and What Patients Should Know

items.q: What is radiofrequency ablation for liver cancer?
items.a: Radiofrequency ablation, or RFA, destroys a liver tumour with heat instead of cutting it out. A doctor guides a thin needle through the skin into the tumour using ultrasound or CT, then passes radio-wave energy through the needle tip. The heat kills the tumour and a small rim of tissue around it. Most patients are sedated rather than fully asleep, and the procedure usually takes under an hour.

items.q: Is my liver tumour small enough for RFA?
items.a: RFA works best for tumours of three centimetres or less, with up to three tumours in the liver. Above that size, heat often cannot reach the whole tumour, and the chance of cancer cells surviving at the edge rises. Position matters as much as size, so tumours sitting next to the bowel, gallbladder or a large blood vessel may be unsuitable. Only your treating team can confirm eligibility after reviewing your scans.

items.q: Why do patients travel to China for liver RFA?
items.a: China treats more liver cancer than any other country, so its major centres perform ablation in very high volume. Zhongshan Hospital and Eastern Hepatobiliary Surgery Hospital, both in Shanghai, are among the best known, with interventional radiology and hepatobiliary surgery teams working side by side. High volume often means shorter waits and more experience with awkward tumour positions, though your own results still depend on your liver function.

items.q: What does liver RFA cost in China?
items.a: Liver RFA in China commonly costs between USD 5,000 and USD 12,000 for the procedure and a short hospital stay. The range depends on the number of tumours, whether CT or ultrasound guidance is used, and whether you also need TACE beforehand. International patient pricing, translation and accommodation are usually quoted separately. Ask the hospital for a written estimate before you travel, as figures can change once your scans are reviewed.

items.q: Is RFA as good as surgery for a small liver tumour?
items.a: For a single tumour under three centimetres, RFA can give survival results close to surgical removal, and it is far easier on the body. Surgery still has the edge for larger tumours and for cases where a wide clear margin matters. Many patients with cirrhosis are not fit for an operation at all, which is why ablation is often chosen. The right answer depends on liver function, tumour position and general health.

items.q: Should I have RFA or microwave ablation?
items.a: Microwave ablation heats tissue faster and is less affected by nearby blood vessels, so many Chinese centres now prefer it for tumours close to large veins. RFA remains well proven and is often chosen for smaller, more accessible tumours. Both use the same needle-through-the-skin approach and the same recovery pattern. Zhongshan Hospital and EHBH offer both, and the interventional radiologist usually picks based on where your tumour sits.

items.q: How long will I need to stay in China for the procedure?
items.a: Plan for roughly two to three weeks in China. The hospital stay itself is usually two to four nights, but you need time beforehand for scans, blood tests and a consultation, and a follow-up scan about four weeks later is often done at home. Most patients walk the same day and feel close to normal within a week. Your team may extend this if TACE is added.

items.q: What can go wrong with liver RFA?
items.a: Serious complications happen in fewer than five percent of liver ablations. The common after-effects are pain at the needle site, mild fever and tiredness for a few days, sometimes called post-ablation syndrome. Rarer problems include bleeding, infection, injury to the bile duct or bowel, and damage to nearby structures. Risk rises when the tumour sits close to the gallbladder or diaphragm, so your team will weigh position carefully.

items.q: What happens if the cancer comes back after RFA?
items.a: RFA can usually be repeated, which is one of its main advantages over surgery. New tumours appear in the liver in a large share of patients within a few years, because the underlying liver disease is still there. Repeat ablation, TACE, or a switch to systemic drugs are all options, depending on how much healthy liver remains. Scans every three to six months are how recurrence is caught early.

items.q: How do I arrange liver RFA at Zhongshan Hospital or EHBH?
items.a: Start by sending recent imaging, liver function results and a pathology or biopsy report, since these decide whether ablation is even possible. The hospital's international office reviews the file and issues an opinion and an estimate, which you then use for the medical visa. CancerFax can help assemble the records and reach the right department, though the final treatment plan always rests with the treating hepatobiliary team.
